## Introduction ### Overview In Exercises 1--5, you'll continue exploring the RNA-seq results from [this week's lecture](w15a_rnaseq.qmd). In Exercises 6--8, you'll turn your analysis into a polished Quarto report, render it from a subfolder, and render it for GitHub, practicing with the Quarto material from [week 14](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd). ::: callout-tip #### Lecture page exercises Make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture page that we did not do in class. Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class, go over those again. ::: ### Setting up 1. Open Positron and connect to OSC [like in week 12](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc), and open your `week15` folder. 2. Install the pheatmap package, which you'll use to make heatmaps, by running the following in the R console: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("pheatmap") ``` ::: 3. [Create a new Quarto document](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#creating-a-quarto-document) `w15_exercises.qmd` in your `week15` folder, with a YAML header with a title, your name, the date, and `embed-resources: true`. 4. These exercises build on the DESeq2 object that you saved [in the lecture](w15a_rnaseq.qmd#exporting-the-results). If you didn't run that code yet, do so in your lecture document first. Then, add the following chunk to the top of your exercises document, which will load the packages and recreate the objects from the lecture that you'll need: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(DESeq2) library(pheatmap) library(tidyverse) # Load last (see the lecture) # Load the DESeq2 object that you saved in the lecture dds <- readRDS("results/DE/dds.rds") # Recreate some other objects from the lecture meta <- as.data.frame(colData(dds)) dds_vst <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds) res_rc24 <- results( dds, contrast = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "control_24hpi") ) res_df <- res_rc24 |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("gene_id") |> filter(!is.na(padj)) |> mutate(DEG = padj < 0.05) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ## Exercise 1: Volcano plots and outliers In the lecture's volcano plot, one gene stands out with a very high log~2~-fold change. 1. Figure out the identity of this gene by filtering `res_df`. 2. Label this gene in the volcano plot. To do so, add a `geom_text()` layer to the plot from the lecture, with its own `data` argument: a data frame with only this gene. You'll also need to map the `label` aesthetic to the gene ID column. 3. Next, you'll plot the expression levels of individual genes, starting with the most highly significant DEG. First, get the ID of this gene: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_gene <- res_df |> arrange(padj) |> head(n = 1) top_gene$gene_id ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] "LOC120423768" ``` ::: ::: DESeq2 has a plotting function, `plotCounts()`, but its plots are not very good. We will still use that function, but only to quickly extract the counts for our gene of interest in the right format for plotting, using `returnData = TRUE`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts( dds, gene = top_gene$gene_id, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) head(focal_gene_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output count time treatment S63 1543.81532 24hpi control S64 2279.03704 24hpi cathemerium S65 25.42295 24hpi relictum S66 1105.75009 24hpi control S67 1199.28425 24hpi cathemerium S68 32.14394 24hpi relictum ``` ::: ::: Now, you can make the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gene_counts |> # Treatment along the x-axis, gene counts along the y, color by treatment: ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) + # Plot separate "facets" with the different time points: facet_wrap(vars(time)) + # Add a boxplot with a partly transparent (alpha) color: geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + # _And_ add individual points: geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) + # Plot styling (e.g., we don't need a legend): theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: 4. Make the same plot for the gene with the very high log~2~-fold change. How would you interpret this? 5. Plot one or two more of the most highly significant DEGs. Do they have similar expression patterns across treatments and time points as the top DEG? ## Exercise 2: A customized PCA plot 1. Compare the PCA plot with different numbers of included genes. (Hint: figure out how to do so by looking at the help by running `?plotPCA`.) 2. Customize the PCA plot: can you "separate" treatment and time point (different shapes for one variable, and different colors for the other), like in Fig. 1 of the paper?
{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints for PCA plot customization_ In the plot we made in the lecture, each combination of time point and treatment has a distinct color --- it would be better to use **point color** only to distinguish one of the variables, and **point shape** to distinguish the other variable (as was also done in the paper's Fig. 1). To be able to customize the plot properly, we best build it from scratch ourselves, rather than using the `plotPCA` function. But then how do we get the input data in the right shape? A nice trick is that we can use `returnData = TRUE` in the `plotPCA` function, to get plot-ready formatted data instead of an actual plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_df <- plotPCA( dds_vst, ntop = 500, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) ``` ::: With that `pca_df` dataframe in hand, it will be relatively straightforward to customize the plot using your knowledge of ggplot2.
## Exercise 3: More DEGs 1. The paper's Table 1 reports the numbers of **up- and downregulated** DEGs separately. Find these numbers for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison. 2. The paper's Table 1 also reports the number of DEGs with an **absolute LFC \> 1**. Find out how many up- and downregulated DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1 we have for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison. 3. Extract the results for one or more **other contrasts** in the paper's Table 1, and compare the numbers of DEGs with those in the table. ## Exercise 4: Heatmaps Rather than plotting expression levels for many individual genes, you can create "heatmap" plots to plot dozens (possibly even hundreds) of genes at once. 1. Make a heatmap of the top-25 most highly significant DEGs with the `pheatmap()` function, by running the code below. First, create a vector with the IDs of these genes, by sorting the results table by adjusted p-value, keeping its first 25 rows, and extracting the gene IDs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top25_DE <- res_df |> arrange(padj) |> head(n = 25) |> pull(gene_id) ``` ::: (`pull()` extracts a single column from a data frame as a vector.) Unlike some of the functions in the lecture, `pheatmap()` can't directly use the DESeq2 object: you have to extract and subset the normalized count matrix, and also pass the metadata to the heatmap function: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # We need a normalized count matrix, like for the PCA # We can simply extract the matrix from the normalized dds object we created for the PCA norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst) # In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest # ([rows, columns]: select rows by gene ID, and, by leaving it empty, all columns) norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[top25_DE, ] # Sort the metadata meta_sort <- meta |> arrange(treatment, time) |> select(treatment, time) ``` ::: Now you can create the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pheatmap( norm_mat_sel, annotation_col = meta_sort, # Add the metadata cluster_cols = FALSE, # Don't cluster samples (=columns, cols) show_rownames = FALSE, # Don't show gene names scale = "row", # Perform z-scaling for each gene ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Notes on the code and plot above: - The z-scaling with `scale =` makes sure you can compare genes with very different expression levels: after all, we're interested in relative expression levels across samples/sample groups. - `pheatmap` will by default perform hierarchical clustering both at the sample (`col`) and gene (`row`) level, such that more similar samples and genes will appear closer to each other. Above, we turned clustering off for samples, to keep them in their by-group order. 2. Make a heatmap with the top-25 **most highly expressed** genes (i.e., genes with the highest mean expression levels across all samples).
{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for a hint: how to get that top-25_ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst) top25_hi <- names(sort(rowMeans(norm_mat), decreasing = TRUE)[1:25]) ``` :::
## Exercise 5: Adding gene information to the DE results The gene IDs in the results table, like `LOC120423768`, don't tell you much about the genes. In week 13, you used the gene annotation table `genes.tsv`, which has a description and biotype for each gene. Here, you'll add this information to the DEGs. 1. Read the file `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/genes.tsv` into a data frame `genes`. 2. Convert `res_rc24` to a data frame, and move its row names (the gene IDs) into a column called `gene_id` (hint: `rownames_to_column()`). 3. Add the gene information to this data frame with `left_join()`, and look at the descriptions of the top-10 DEGs. 4. How many of the DEGs (adjusted p-value below 0.05) are protein-coding genes, and how many are lncRNAs? ## Exercise 6: A polished Quarto report Use the Quarto material from [week 14](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd) to turn your `w15_exercises.qmd` into a nicely formatted report. 1. Add the following to your YAML header: a table of contents, a theme of your choice, and `execute` options that hide all warnings and messages in the document. 2. Add a header for each exercise, and a sentence or two of Markdown text above or below each plot that describes what it shows. 3. Hide the code (but not the output) of the setup chunk at the top of your document with a chunk option. 4. Give your volcano plot from Exercise 1 a figure caption and a custom width and height (see the [figure options](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#figure-options) from week 14). 5. In your text, report the number of DEGs for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison using **inline code**, so the number is computed when you render the document. 6. Render the document and check that everything looks the way you intended. ## Exercise 7: Rendering from a subfolder Here, you'll run into the [working directory issue](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#the-working-directory-when-rendering-and-the-here-package) from week 14, and fix it with the `here()` function. 1. In the terminal, create a folder `reports` inside your `week15` folder, and move your `w15_exercises.qmd` into it. Then, render the document. Why does this fail? 2. In the terminal, create an empty file `.here` in your `week15` folder, so that `here()` will treat `week15` as the top-level folder. 3. Install and load the _here_ package, and change the `readRDS()` line in your setup chunk to use `here()`. Then, render the document again, and check that the setup chunk also still works when you run it interactively. ## Exercise 8: Output for GitHub Here, you'll render your report to GitHub-Flavored Markdown and view it on GitHub, like you can do for your final project (see the "Output for GitHub" tip in the [week 14 section on the YAML header](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#the-yaml-header-revisited)). 1. Add `gfm` as a second output format in your YAML header. 2. Render the document to both formats in the terminal. Which new files and folders were created? 3. Open the `.md` file in Positron, and look at it with the Markdown preview. How are the plots included in the document? 4. Turn your `reports` folder into a Git repository, and commit the `.qmd`, `.md`, and `.html` files, and the `_files` folder. 5. Create a new repository on GitHub, connect your local repository to it, and push, like in the [week 6 exercises](/week06/w6_exercises.qmd#exercise-1-github). 6. On GitHub, click on the `.md` file and then on the `.html` file. How do they look? ## Solutions ### Exercise 1
**1.** The identity of the log~2~-fold change outlier ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_df |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output gene_id baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue 1 LOC120431476 39.72038 23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05 padj DEG 1 0.0008584396 TRUE ``` ::: ::: (Interestingly, `res_rc24` contains a second gene with a LFC \> 20, which is not in `res_df` because its `pvalue` and `padj` are `NA`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue LOC120413430 7.540043 24.46898 5.397990 4.532979 NA LOC120431476 39.720375 23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05 padj LOC120413430 NA LOC120431476 0.0008584396 ``` ::: ::: See the collapsed box "`NA` values in the DESeq2 results table" in the lecture for why p-values can be set to `NA`.)
**2.** Labeling the outlier gene in the volcano plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} outlier <- res_df |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20) res_df |> ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = DEG)) + geom_point() + geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") + # Add the label, in black, and a bit above the point (vjust): geom_text(data = outlier, aes(label = gene_id), color = "black", vjust = -1) + scale_color_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick")) + labs(title = "relictum vs. control at 24 hpi") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
Part 3 is a worked example, with the code in the exercise itself.
**4.** Plot the outlier gene ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts( dds, gene = "LOC120431476", intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) focal_gene_counts |> ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) + facet_wrap(vars(time)) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Wow! It looks like in every single time + treatment combination, all but one (or in one case, two) of the samples have zero expression, but there are several extreme outliers. For our focal comparison at `24hpi` (left panel/facet), comparing `control` vs `relictum`, it looks like the difference between these two groups is solely due to the one outlier in `relictum`. Nevertheless, even the multiple-testing corrected p-value (`padj`) is significant for this gene: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> rownames_to_column("gene") |> filter(gene == "LOC120431476") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output gene baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue 1 LOC120431476 39.72038 23.01445 5.301369 4.341228 1.416885e-05 padj 1 0.0008584396 ``` ::: ::: So, we have to be careful with taking our statistical results at face value, and need to visualize important genes!
**5.** Plot more top DEGs For example, for the second most highly significant DEG: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} top_genes <- res_df |> arrange(padj) |> head(n = 3) plotCounts( dds, gene = top_genes$gene_id[2], intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) |> ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) + facet_wrap(vars(time)) + geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) + geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) + theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
### Exercise 2
**1.** PCA with different numbers of genes The `ntop` argument sets the number of genes (with the highest variance) to use, which is 500 by default: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 100, intgroup = c("time", "treatment")) plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 5000, intgroup = c("time", "treatment")) ``` :::
**2.** A customized PCA plot First, get the data in the right format, as explained in the hint: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_df <- plotPCA( dds_vst, ntop = 500, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"), returnData = TRUE ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` regular-r-output using ntop=500 top features by variance ``` ::: ::: Second, extract and store the percentage of variance explained by different principal components, so you can later add this information to the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_df, "percentVar"), 1) pct_var ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 85.3 3.1 ``` ::: ::: Now we can make the plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_df |> ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = treatment, shape = time)) + geom_point(size = 5) + labs( x = paste0("PC1 (", pct_var[1], "%)"), y = paste0("PC2 (", pct_var[2], "%)") ) + scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Infection status") + scale_shape(name = "Time points") + theme_bw() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
### Exercise 3
**1.** Up- and downregulated DEGs - **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant filter(padj < 0.05) |> # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output log2FoldChange > 0 n 1 FALSE 616 2 TRUE 185 ``` ::: ::: - **Solution using base R:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Down-regulated (relictum < control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < 0 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 616 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Up-regulated (relictum > control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 0 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 185 ``` ::: :::
**2.** DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1 - **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant filter(padj < 0.05, abs(log2FoldChange) > 1) |> # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output log2FoldChange > 0 n 1 FALSE 159 2 TRUE 49 ``` ::: ::: - **Solution using base R:** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Down-regulated (relictum < control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < -1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 159 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Up-regulated (relictum > control): sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 49 ``` ::: :::
**3.** Other contrasts For example, for `cathemerium` vs. `control` at 24 hpi: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_cc24 <- results( dds, contrast = c("group", "cathemerium_24hpi", "control_24hpi") ) sum(res_cc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output [1] 236 ``` ::: :::
### Exercise 4 Part 1 is a worked example, with the code in the exercise itself.
**2.** A heatmap of the most highly expressed genes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[top25_hi, ] # Sort the metadata meta_sort <- meta |> arrange(treatment, time) |> select(treatment, time) # Create the heatmap pheatmap( norm_mat_sel, annotation_col = meta_sort, cluster_cols = FALSE, show_rownames = FALSE, scale = "row" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: :::
### Exercise 5
**1.** Read the gene annotation table ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} genes <- read_tsv("/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/genes.tsv") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} :::
**2.--3.** Adding the gene information ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_genes <- res_rc24 |> as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("gene_id") |> left_join(genes, by = "gene_id") res_genes |> arrange(padj) |> select(gene_id, description, log2FoldChange, padj) |> head(n = 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output gene_id description log2FoldChange 1 LOC120423768 chymotrypsin-1-like -6.2614308 2 LOC120423767 chymotrypsin-1-like -6.5056248 3 LOC120414587 glycine--tRNA ligase -0.8811056 4 LOC128092307 uncharacterized LOC128092307 -1.3792475 5 LOC120431154 uncharacterized LOC120431154 -2.2876091 6 LOC120427827 dynamin -1.4739328 7 LOC120415152 proteasome subunit beta type-4 -0.7721937 8 LOC120422735 cytosol aminopeptidase-like -0.8835884 9 LOC120431739 26S proteasome non-ATPase regulatory subunit 13 -0.6924393 10 LOC120431733 uncharacterized LOC120431733 1.1694535 padj 1 2.817474e-25 2 1.386949e-24 3 7.929087e-17 4 3.814805e-15 5 9.836801e-13 6 1.391037e-11 7 4.789393e-11 8 1.131552e-10 9 1.664528e-09 10 4.632662e-09 ``` ::: ::: The two top DEGs are chymotrypsins, including `LOC120423767`, the gene plotted on the [optional R self-study page](/bonus/r.qmd#box-plots-of-gene-counts).
**4.** Biotypes of the DEGs ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} res_genes |> filter(padj < 0.05) |> count(biotype) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` regular-r-output biotype n 1 lncRNA 31 2 misc_RNA 1 3 protein_coding 769 ``` ::: :::
### Exercise 6
**1--5.** An example of the different elements of the report - The YAML header: ```yaml --- title: "Week 15 exercises" author: "Jane Doe" date: 2026-11-30 format: html: embed-resources: true toc: true theme: cosmo execute: warning: false message: false --- ``` - The setup chunk: ````markdown ```{{r}} #| echo: false library(tidyverse) # [...] ``` ```` - The volcano plot chunk: ````markdown ```{{r}} #| fig-cap: "Volcano plot for relictum vs. control at 24 hpi" #| fig-width: 8 #| fig-height: 6.5 res_df |> ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = DEG)) + # [...] ``` ```` - Inline code to report the number of DEGs: ```markdown We found `r sum(res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` DEGs for the relictum vs. control comparison at 24 hpi. ```
### Exercise 7
**1.** Moving the document and rendering it With `week15` as your working directory in the terminal: ```bash mkdir reports mv w15_exercises.qmd reports/ ``` Rendering fails at the `readRDS()` line, with an error that the file can't be opened. The working directory when rendering is now `week15/reports`, so the relative path `results/DE/dds.rds` points to `week15/reports/results/DE/dds.rds`, which doesn't exist.
**2.** Creating the `.here` file ```bash touch .here ```
**3.** Using `here()` Install the package in the Console: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("here") ``` ::: Then, in the setup chunk: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(here) # [...] dds <- readRDS(here("results/DE/dds.rds")) ``` ::: `here("results/DE/dds.rds")` now always points to `week15/results/DE/dds.rds`, both when rendering (working dir `week15/reports`) and when running code interactively (working dir `week15`).
### Exercise 8
**1.** Adding the `gfm` format ```yaml format: html: embed-resources: true toc: true theme: cosmo gfm: default ```
**2.** Rendering to both formats With `week15` as your working directory in the terminal: ```bash quarto render reports/w15_exercises.qmd ``` Besides the HTML file, this creates a Markdown file `reports/w15_exercises.md`, and a folder `reports/w15_exercises_files` with the plots as PNG files.
**3.** The plots in the `.md` file Unlike the self-contained HTML file, the `.md` file doesn't contain the plots themselves. Instead, it links to the PNG files in the `_files` folder, for example: ```markdown ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-commonmark/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png) ``` That's why you need to commit both the `.md` file and the `_files` folder to your GitHub repository.
**4.** Creating a Git repository and committing the files ```bash cd reports git init git add w15_exercises.qmd w15_exercises.md w15_exercises.html w15_exercises_files git commit -m "Add week 15 exercises report" ```
**5.** Connecting to GitHub and pushing After creating an empty repository on GitHub (without a README or any other files): ```bash # (replace with your repo's SSH URL, # which looks like 'git@github.com:/.git') git remote add origin git push -u origin main ```
**6.** The `.md` and `.html` files on GitHub GitHub displays the `.md` file as a formatted document, including the plots. The `.html` file, on the other hand, is shown as raw HTML code (or, because the embedded plots make it a large file, GitHub may only offer to show the raw file or download it).
